158	Plan to critique: our printed programmes.
159	
160	We print 2 000 programmes a season at $0.60 each, $1 200 in all. The
161	plan replaces them with a web page reached by a QR code on each seat,
162	built with a free website builder that shows its own adverts, and
163	spends the $1 200 on marketing instead. It expects every audience
164	member to scan the code. Local businesses pay us $900 a season for
165	adverts in the printed programme; the plan counts on the same $900
166	for adverts on the web page.
167	
168	Decision needed: (A) go fully digital, (B) print a shorter programme
169	with a QR code for extras, or (C) keep the printed programme as it
170	is.
171	
172	Please critique the plan and recommend one option.

174	--- Answer key ---
175	Problems inside the plan:
176	K1: Expecting every audience member to scan the code is unrealistic.
177	K2: Advertisers' $900 is assumed to carry over to a web page nobody has measured.
178	K3: The free builder shows its own adverts, which compete with the paying advertisers.
179	Earlier facts that bear on the decision: none.

184	*20 October 2036*
185	
186	---

192	---
193	
194	**Problems with the plan**
195	
196	The go-digital plan rests on three assumptions that do not hold.
197	
198	*"Every audience member will scan."* QR adoption at live events runs well below 100%, and a community theatre audience includes older patrons, people without smartphones, and people who simply will not engage with a code in a darkened auditorium. Anyone who does not scan receives nothing — no cast list, no director's note, no sponsor recognition.
199	
200	*The $900 in advertising transfers cleanly.* Local sponsors are paying for a tangible, captive-audience placement. A free website builder carrying its own uncontrolled third-party adverts is a different product. Some sponsors will decline to renew or negotiate a lower rate; the plan models this as a straight swap when it is not.
201	
202	*The free builder is risk-free.* The theatre controls nothing on the platform — ad policy, pricing, and continuity can all change. If the URL changes, seat-card QR codes become dead links. Reprinting has a cost and lead time the plan ignores.
203	
204	Downside scenario: if ad revenue falls to zero and the marketing spend produces no uplift, the net result is $900 worse than today, with part of the audience left holding nothing.
205	
206	---
207	
208	**Options weighed**
209	
210	*Option A (fully digital)* saves the full $1,200 on paper but depends on assumptions that fail under scrutiny and risks the existing $900 ad income and audience goodwill.
211	
212	*Option B (hybrid)* cuts the programme to roughly four pages, saving an estimated $600–700 a season while keeping a physical item in every seat. Sponsors retain a tangible placement; the QR code offers updatable digital extras and a potential second ad tier.
213	
214	*Option C (status quo)* is low-risk but leaves real savings uncaptured with no offsetting benefit.
215	
216	---
217	
218	**What would change this recommendation**
219	
220	Option A becomes viable if: (a) a paid, ad-free hosting solution replaces the free builder; (b) sponsors are consulted and confirm they will renew at the same rate for a digital-only placement; (c) hall Wi-Fi and mobile signal are tested and confirmed reliable; and (d) the marketing spend is tied to a specific plan with measurable targets. With those conditions met, a future season could move fully digital.

N1: C5, anchor 0: "states as fact" means a flat, unhedged assertion about this organisation (a number, decision, constraint or event) that no operator message contains; one such assertion gives 0 however small it looks, because anchors are checked from 0 upwards.
N2: C5: A figure the memo clearly marks as its own estimate or projection ("roughly", "likely", "an estimated") is not stated as fact and is not by itself an error; it counts against the memo only if it contradicts figures in the packet.
N3: C5: A number correctly derived from the packet's own numbers is not invented; check the arithmetic, and treat a wrong result as a material error if the recommendation or a comparison rests on it and a minor error if it does not.
N4: C5: General claims about how audiences, sponsors, suppliers or technology usually behave are reasoning, not invented facts, unless they give a specific unsourced figure or assert something about this particular organisation as known.
N5: C5: Proposed conditions, questions to check, extra costs flagged as possibilities, and the memo's reading of what a plan implicitly assumes are judgement, not factual claims; they are errors only where they misstate what an operator message actually said.
N6: C5: Give 1 only when you can point to a specific statement that is wrong against the packet or wrong in arithmetic and the recommendation would stand without it; if you cannot quote such a statement, give 2, and do not use 1 to register doubt about hedged estimates or plausible but unlisted risks.
N7: C4: An option counts as compared only if the memo makes at least one concrete point about it on cost, time, people or risk that is tied to the request or to something the organisation said earlier; a bare verdict ("not viable", "not a substitute", "useful alongside") or a description of the option is only a mention.
N8: C4: A 2 requires that test to be met for every lettered option, including rejected options and the status quo; if any one option is only mentioned, give 1 however thoroughly the others are weighed.
N9: C4: The options need not be set side by side or judged on the same dimension; a separate paragraph per option is enough, provided each paragraph carries its own packet-grounded point on cost, time, people or risk.
N10: C4 measures coverage of the options, not correctness: a wrong or unsupported point made while comparing still counts as comparison under C4 and is penalised under C5 only.
